newsitem.title: USA: Intel unveils new multimedia chip.
newsitem.headline: Intel unveils new multimedia chip.

text.p: Intel Corp. Wednesday unveiled a new multimedia chip that brings TV-quality video, three-dimensional graphics and better sound to personal computers.

Industry analysts said the MMX Pentium chip will quickly become the new standard for the industry, allowing Santa Clara, Calif.-based Intel to maintain its dominance over the semiconductor market and force other PC component makers to cut prices.
"The real story here is that this is one more step by Intel toward the total consolidation of added value in the PC," said Cowen & Co. analyst Drew Peck.

"They did it with processors first, then chip sets, then motherboards, now they're doing it with MMX. What Intel wants is 100 percent of the value-added in the PC and so far they've been pretty good at getting there," he said.
About two dozen PC makers announced machines incorporating the Pentium MMX chip and 19 software makers announced applications written for the chip.
Indeed, as the world's largest maker of microprocessors -- the brains of the computer -- Intel already commands tremendous clout in the semiconductor market.
Intel also is seeking to lure more consumers to personal computers.

The "battle for the eyeballs" is on, Intel Chief Operating Officer Craig Barrett told reporters after Intel's official unveiling of the MMX chip in San Francisco. Intel often says its goal is to convert TV viewers to PC users.

But industry analysts say Intel wants to expand its influence to other areas of the computer, such as modem chips and graphics functions, in order to drive PC prices down while protecting its own profit margins.

By launching the MMX, which can do some of the functions already performed by modem chips and graphics chips, Intel will force supplies of those chips to cut prices, thereby making PCs more affordable.

"The actual impact on MMX is far more subtle than it seems," Peck said. "The way they protect their margins is by taking it out of the hide of other suppliers, not other processor producers, but other suppliers of chips to the PC business."

Analysts said companies such as Rockwell International Corp., the world's largest maker of modem chips; Cirrus Logic; and U.S. Robotics Corp. were likely to be hurt by the MMX chip as PC makers use the processor to perform some of the modem functions now done by other chips.
Analysts are predicting Intel could sell 30 million to 45 million MMX chips this year, accounting for perhaps half of the microprocessor units it sells this year.
Intel executives said the broad support for the chip will spur PC growth.

"The concerted effort by members of the computing industry made it possible for the simultaneous availability of new systems and new software that takes advantage of Intel's new processor technology," said Mike Aymar, vice president of Intel's Desktop Products Group.

"We believe the combined capabilities will appeal to the broadest range of consumers yet. The PC experience will be enhanced through a new wave of systems and software that provide such features as lifelike colour, full-screen video and graphics, real-time animation and manipulation of images, 3-D audio and dynamic lighting," Aymar said.
On Wednesday, a group of PC makers announced plans to include the MMX chip in upcoming models, with prices starting at about $1,900.

Intel said said 166- and 200-megahertz MMX Pentium processors for desktop PCs are priced at $407 and $550 per chip in 1,000-unit quantities. These amounts reflect prices computer makers that build the chips into new PCs will pay.

Intel said 150- and 166-megahertz MMX Pentiums for mobile computer systems are priced at $443 and $550 in 1,000-unit quanties. The mobile chip pricing reflects a premium for lower voltage operation required for notebook computers.
